title: Everyone says habits take 21 days. That number came from a book about mental images.
description:
That number came from a book about mental images. Maxwell Maltz's 1960 book Psycho-Cybernetics said it takes a minimum of about 21 days for a mental image to change, drawing on plastic surgery recovery and phantom limbs.

96 volunteers picked a new daily habit, such as eating fruit with lunch, and rated how automatic it felt over 84 days.

The average time for a habit to feel automatic. Individuals ranged from 18 days to a forecast 254.

Was a forecast. The study stopped at 84 days, so the longest time was projected, not observed.

Barely mattered. One missed day had little effect on later progress. Many missed days, added up, lowered how automatic the habit became.

Roughly two months, with a very wide range.

Sources:
- https://blogs.ucl.ac.uk/bsh/2012/06/29/busting-the-21-days-habit-formation-myth/: read. Established Maltz's 1960 book Psycho-Cybernetics saying it takes a minimum of about 21 days to effect any perceptible change in a mental image, based on examples like plastic surgery recovery and phantom limbs rather than habit research; the Lally study tracking people for 84 days; an average of 66 days for the habit to form; one person at 18 days; and another forecast at 254 days.
- https://bps.org.uk/research-digest/how-form-habit: read. Corroborated 96 recruited and 82 completing, the 84 day study length, the 66 day average to maximum automaticity, the 18 to 254 day range with 254 extrapolated beyond the study end, and that a single missed day had little effect on later gains while many missed repetitions cumulatively lowered the automaticity reached.
- https://www.spring.org.uk/?p=107834 and https://jamesclear.com/new-habit: read. Corroborated 96 UCL participants, the 66 day average, the 18 to 254 day range, Maltz's 21 day claim and that the 254 figure is an estimate because the study ran only 12 weeks.
